## Access is a timing problem {.statement}

The building can be nearby and still be unavailable when people need it.

## The research question {.question}

Do later weekday closing times change evening visits?

## A small interrupted series

This **synthetic** example follows one library for six weeks.

| Period | Closing time | Mean evening visits |
|---|---:|---:|
| Weeks 1–3 | 18:00 | 42 |
| Weeks 4–6 | 20:00 | 67 |

The design demonstrates a talk structure; it does not support a causal claim.

# From timing to observed visits

## Visits rose after the schedule changed {.visual}

![Synthetic weekly evening visits. The dashed line marks the change to a later closing time.](figure.svg){#fig-visits fig-alt="Evening visits are 38, 43, and 45 before extended hours, then 61, 67, and 72 afterward. A dashed vertical line separates weeks three and four."}

## Read the figure before the coefficient {.statement}

The visible change is large; the design is too weak to identify why it happened.

## What this example teaches

- State what is observed.
- Separate description from identification.
- Give the main figure a whole slide.

The visual uses a layered graphical grammar [@wickham2010].

## The next study needs a comparison {.question}

Which similar libraries did **not** extend their hours?
